tagline: Stone ruins, big skies, great falls
overview:
Zimbabwe is a landlocked country in southern Africa, a little larger than Montana, spread across a high plateau between the Zambezi River in the north and the Limpopo in the south. The Zambezi plunges over Victoria Falls on the border with Zambia, and Lake Kariba, one of the world's largest reservoirs, stretches along the same frontier. Harare, the capital, sits on cool high ground in the northeast.

About 16 million people live in Zimbabwe. English is an official language used in schools and government, alongside Shona and Ndebele, which most people speak at home; the constitution recognizes sixteen languages in all, including sign language. Zimbabwe is a republic. The country takes its name from Great Zimbabwe, a medieval city whose name means houses of stone, and its national emblem is a soapstone bird carved there centuries ago. Mining, tobacco farming and tourism are the main industries.
landAndNature: Most of Zimbabwe lies on the highveld, a broad plateau above 1,200 meters where the air stays pleasant most of the year. The Eastern Highlands along the Mozambique border are cooler and often misty, with pine forests, tea estates and Mount Nyangani, the highest point at 2,592 meters. Hotter, lower country spreads to the south. Balancing rocks, huge granite boulders left stacked by erosion, stand across the country and appear on the banknotes. Hwange National Park holds one of Africa's largest elephant populations, along with lions, giraffes and painted wild dogs. Baobab trees, some over a thousand years old, store water in their swollen trunks.
peopleAndCulture: Sadza, a stiff maize porridge, is the daily food, eaten with relish of vegetables, beans or stewed beef. Zimbabwean sculptors have made the country famous: Shona stone carvers shape serpentine and springstone into smooth human and animal forms shown in galleries worldwide. Music centers on the mbira, a thumb piano of metal keys played inside a gourd, whose rippling patterns accompany ceremonies honoring ancestors; chimurenga music grew out of those rhythms. Soccer is the biggest sport, and Zimbabwe's cricket team plays international matches. The swimmer Kirsty Coventry won seven Olympic medals, more than any other African swimmer.
history: Farming and cattle-keeping peoples built Great Zimbabwe between roughly 1100 and 1450, a city of mortarless stone walls that traded gold and ivory with the Indian Ocean coast; perhaps 10,000 people lived there at its height. Shona and later Ndebele states ruled the plateau afterward. In the 1890s Cecil Rhodes's British South Africa Company seized the land, which became the colony of Southern Rhodesia, and white settlers took the best farmland. A white minority government declared independence in 1965, and a liberation war followed until majority rule and recognized independence came on April 18, 1980, with Robert Mugabe leading. He governed for 37 years, during which land seizures and hyperinflation wrecked the economy, and he was removed in 2017.
funFacts: Zimbabwe printed a 100-trillion-dollar banknote during hyperinflation in 2008; it is now sold mainly as a souvenir.
The walls of Great Zimbabwe were built without any mortar, the stones fitted so tightly they have stood for 700 years.
The Zimbabwe bird, carved from soapstone at Great Zimbabwe long ago, appears on the national flag and coins.
Hwange National Park shelters tens of thousands of elephants, one of the largest concentrations anywhere in Africa.
Spray from Victoria Falls can be seen from 50 kilometers away, which is why the falls are called the smoke that thunders.
